The post The return of the crammer: private ownership and the missing data in legal education appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Dr Omar Mashjari, Associate Professor of Law and Head of the School of Law and Criminology at Liverpool Hope University, writing in a personal capacity.

In August, Matt Innes set out on this blog the case for Lincoln Bishop University joining Global University Systems (GUS). A new company in the group will run the university, and a charitable foundation will act as trustee of its founding endowments. Spencer Withrington notes that Lincoln Bishop would be the first English public university to pass into for-profit ownership.

The model has a precedent in legal education. In 2012, the College of Law, which the Law Society had formed in 1962 to train solicitors, sold its teaching business to Montagu Private Equity for about £200 million. The charity kept the proceeds and became the Legal Education Foundation. The degree-awarding powers went with the business, which gained university title in November 2012 as the University of Law. Times Higher Education called it the UK’s first for-profit university. Its first accounts recorded £177 million owed to other companies in its group. Montagu sold the university to GUS in 2015. Jim Dickinson has since described the result as ‘degree-awarding powers as an asset class’.

An old market restored

The Solicitors Qualifying Examination (SQE), introduced in 2021, opened the preparation of solicitors to any provider. Its design recalls the nineteenth century, when the Law Society examined candidates and commercial tutors known as crammers prepared them for a fee. The best known, Gibson and Weldon, merged with the Society’s own school in 1962 to form the College of Law. The University of Law now dates its origins to the firm’s formation in 1876.

Today the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA) sets a single examination. It states that it does ‘not regulate training providers that offer SQE courses’. Anyone may sell preparation, and public money meets part of the cost. Providers place SQE preparation inside master’s degrees that attract postgraduate loans, and students at investor-owned universities can take tuition fee loans for their law degrees.

Choosing without the data

A student buys such a course once and learns its value only when the results arrive. Such a market depends on published results.

When the Legal Services Board (LSB) approved the SQE in 2020, the SRA undertook to publish pass rates by training provider. In March 2025 the LSB said it expected the data ‘by autumn 2025 at the latest’. In December 2025 the SRA said it had ‘not had confidence in the quality of the data collected’. Candidates must now report how they prepared before seeing their results. Five years after launch, the SRA has published no pass rates by provider.

Results are also unequal. In the January 2025 sitting of SQE1, the first of the examination’s two parts, White candidates sitting for the first time passed at a rate of 70 per cent. The rates were 49 per cent for Asian or Asian British candidates and 37 per cent for Black or Black British candidates.

The missing data matter most to candidates who pay for themselves. Research for the SRA found that under the old system employers paid the vocational course fees of 45 per cent of White students. The figures for Asian and Black students were 24 and 26 per cent. Candidates who fund themselves choose on price and marketing claims.

The law degree still counts

Analysis by Kaplan, the SRA’s assessment provider, found that university rank explained more of the variation in SQE1 scores than any other factor it measured. The choice of university therefore matters, and law recruitment is rising. UCAS recorded 28,590 applicants placed on law courses on results day in 2026, up from 24,590 in 2024.

The for-profit universities have grown faster still. Higher Education Statistics Agency data show the University of Law growing from 8,350 students in 2017/18 to 19,730 in 2024/25, BPP from 10,005 to 31,490 and Arden University from 3,700 to 32,740. On Withrington’s reading of the latest outcome data, each of the three falls below at least one minimum threshold set by the Office for Students (OfS) for continuation, completion or progression. These figures cover all subjects. The OfS does not publish law outcomes grouped by type of owner.

What regulators should do

Over two in five providers forecast a deficit for 2025-26. More governing bodies will therefore weigh offers of private capital, and two obvious reforms would let students and policymakers test what that capital delivers. The SRA could publish pass rates by training provider and by the university where each candidate took a first degree, with context on each provider’s intake. It promised the first of these in 2020. In addition, the OfS should publish outcomes for each subject by type of owner, measured against benchmarks. When a provider changes ownership, it should also publish its assessment of how the purchase is financed and what debt the institution will carry. At present, the OfS decides whether a new company may register and hold degree-awarding powers and university title but it does not approve or block the change of ownership itself (though it does assess the provider’s financial sustainability).

Both regulators already collect most of the data needed. They should publish them before the next university changes hands.

title: Fixing UK’s youth jobs crisis demands much more investment, TUC boss warns
summary:
Paul Nowak also calls on government to avoid arbitrary benefit cuts before much-anticipated Milburn report is published this week

Fixing Britain’s youth jobs crisis will require ministers to drastically increase investment in employment support while avoiding arbitrary cuts to benefits, the head of the trade union movement has said.

Before an important official report expected next week, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, Paul Nowak, said the government had a “once in a generation chance” to secure young people’s futures.

full_text:
Fixing Britain’s youth jobs crisis will require ministers to drastically increase investment in employment support while avoiding arbitrary cuts to benefits, the head of the trade union movement has said.

Before an important official report expected next week, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, Paul Nowak, said the government had a “once in a generation chance” to secure young people’s futures.

In an interview with the Guardian before the highly anticipated Milburn review into young people and work, he said the costs of increasing job support, education and training would be outweighed by economic gains that would help to ease the pressure on the welfare state.

“There is no solution that is cost-free,” he said. “The government is going to have to be prepared to invest in securing the future of those young people, but also to invest to secure what is the future of our economy.

“This is where the government is going to have to be clear. Of course as a country it’s right to invest in our physical infrastructure, but also we have to invest in social infrastructure too.”

Ministers are braced for the report by Alan Milburn, the former Labour health secretary, to recommend welfare cuts to fund job support for almost a million young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet).

The report was delayed until after the budget amid fears that the call for welfare cuts would sit uneasily alongside the tax and spending plans of the chancellor, John Healey.

Andy Burnham has said the surge in young people who are Neet is an “economic catastrophe and a moral failure” and that tougher benefits rules and more help for young people will form part of his government’s response to the Milburn report.

The prime minister has been at pains to take a cautious approach to avoid a repeat of the welfare rebellion, which forced Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves into an embarrassing and costly U-turn on planned disability benefit cuts within a year of coming to power.

Calling on Burnham to focus on delivering a step change in employment support, Nowak said increased investment would help to bring down the benefits bill by getting more young people into work.

“We can’t afford to not do this stuff, as the benefits bill will go up if young people are not supported,” he said.

“I don’t think this government is going to repeat the mistake of the previous attempt at benefit reform, where you make arbitrary cuts, [and] where you have an impact on some of the most vulnerable people without thinking about how you support people into work.”

There is rising concern over youth worklessness. Most Britons now see the youth jobs crisis as one of the biggest problems facing the country – ranking it second only to the cost of living and above NHS waiting lists, housing, crime and immigration, according to polling by the research company Focaldata for the Jobs Foundation.

The employment charity, co-founded by the Conservative peer Matthew Elliott, is behind a national campaign to tackle worklessness that launches on Monday. It includes a pledge, backed by a group of leading employers – including Amazon, Pret a Manger, NatWest, Marks & Spencer and Shell – that have committed to support young people who have been overlooked for work.

A government spokesperson said: “We are determined to turn the tide on youth unemployment which has been years in the making.

“We have already pledged £2.5bn in youth employment support, which will deliver almost 500,000 opportunities to earn and learn, while engaging with business including some of Britain’s biggest retail and hospitality brands to create up to 200,000 jobs for young people.

“Further reform will follow the Milburn review, which will be published in the autumn.”

title: Teaching GCSE topics younger risks turning schools into ‘early exam factories’, Powell warns
summary:
Lucy Powell says proposals to end widespread practice will be included in overhaul of England’s national curriculum

Pushing GCSE subjects on younger pupils risks turning England’s secondary schools into “early exam factories”, the education secretary has said, warning that it is increasing disengagement from education.

Lucy Powell wants schools to end the widespread practice of teaching GCSE topics to pupils in year 9 or earlier, before they officially start in year 10, and says she plans to reduce the amount of GCSE content to make it easier to fit into the official timetable.

full_text:
Pushing GCSE subjects on younger pupils risks turning England’s secondary schools into “early exam factories”, the education secretary has said, warning that it is increasing disengagement from education.

Lucy Powell wants schools to end the widespread practice of teaching GCSE topics to pupils in year 9 or earlier, before they officially start in year 10, and says she plans to reduce the amount of GCSE content to make it easier to fit into the official timetable.

The Department for Education (DfE) said the proposals would be included in the government’s overhaul of the national curriculum to be published in early 2027, as part of its plans to tackle school disengagement as well as the disadvantage gap between pupils from rich and poor backgrounds and the rising number of young people not in education, employment or training.

Powell said: “The early years of secondary school should be a time when children are excited to go to school and engage in the specialist and much broader teaching on offer, and where they find their passion and develop a love of learning.

“Instead, we’ve seen worrying trends of disengagement and high levels of persistent absence, with the disadvantage gap stubbornly large and too many leaving school without the knowledge and skills they need to thrive.

“That’s what our exciting and engaging new national curriculum aims to address as part of our wider education reforms.

“What’s more, the pressures of GCSEs and an overcrowded curriculum are resulting in too many children receiving a narrower offer … and being rushed towards exams without grasping the fundamentals or developing deeper understanding. I’m putting a stop to that.”

Many secondary schools start introducing GCSE-level material to pupils in year 9 as a way of spreading out the course content. But Powell told the Sunday Times she was opposed to “early exam factories” and that plans to reduce GCSEs’ content would enable the courses to be taught comfortably within the allotted two years of year 10 and year 11.

The new curriculum will say schools “should not start GCSE specifications early for large cohorts or see children routinely required to narrow their options earlier or entered earlier for exams”, the DfE stated.

However, the new policy will not be compulsory, and schools will retain the flexibility to teach GCSEs to younger students whom they judge to be capable of coping with it.

Powell said slimmed-down GCSEs would give schools “more time to develop deeper understanding, as well as a richer experience that will engage more young people in their passions and prepare them better for the fast-changing world they will grow up in”.

Powell also said she supported new efforts to help the government and other groups improve educational outcomes for children from white working-class communities.

“A child’s background should never mean opportunity belongs to someone else,” she said.

“But right now, too many white working-class children are falling behind at every stage of their education.”

title: Secondary schools told to stop teaching GCSEs before Year 10
summary: The government says pupils in Year 7 to 9 should have "richer, more engaging" learning than preparing for GCSEs.
full_text:
Secondary schools will be told not to teach GCSEs early as part of a major shake-up of how children in Years 7 to 9 are taught.

The government plans to make Key Stage 3 a more distinct education phase, urging schools to focus less on exams and more on a "richer, more engaging" experience.

The changes come in response to two reviews that found pupils were increasingly becoming disengaged in their early teenage years, affecting attendance and achievement, the Department for Education (DfE) said.

The move will mark a reversal of the approach taken by the previous Conservative government to focus the first three years of secondary school on core subjects and on doing well in assessments.

Former Education Secretary Michael Gove prioritised English, maths and science, while raising grade boundaries, making exams harder and limiting resits.

He also made GCSEs linear, meaning they are sat all in one go at the end of Year 11 instead of over the course of Key Stage 4.

These reforms meant teachers started preparing pupils for exams at an earlier stage at the expense of teaching unexamined parts of their subject.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said: "The early years of secondary school should be a time when children are excited to go to school and engage in the specialist and much broader teaching on offer, and where they find their passion and develop a love of learning."

She added that ringfencing Key Stage 3 studies would allow for "more time to develop deeper understanding, as well as a richer experience that will engage more young people in their passions".

The DfE has pledged a "more engaging offer" in subjects like drama, PE, music and languages, which have seen a decline in students taking them, when it publishes its new curriculum later this year.

It says persistent absence nearly doubles among pupils between Year 6 and Year 9, from 13% to 15%.

The department pointed to a recent survey commissioned by the International Baccalaureate that found GCSE prep dominated Key Stage 3 learning in England, with 57% of teachers saying it was the leading influence on the curriculum.

"The pressures of GCSEs and an overcrowded curriculum are resulting in too many children receiving a narrower offer during Key Stage 3 and being rushed towards exams without grasping the fundamentals or developing deeper understanding," Powell said. "I'm putting a stop to that."

A 2015 Ofsted report suggested that Key Stage 3 may be "wasted years", echoing the view at the time that pupils aged 11-14 lacked a clear motivation to work hard.

However, the government faced criticism at the time that its reforms made each exam far more significant, meaning teachers refocused lessons only on what could come up in them.

Reacting to the DfE's announcement on Sunday, Lib Dem education spokeswoman Munira Wilson MP said school was "more than drilling kids for exams" but cautioned against "micromanaging" teachers.

She added that a new curriculum "alone won't get children back into the classroom", noting that "too many pupils are missing school because of anxiety and unmet mental health needs" while "schools can't offer more drama, music and languages without the teachers to teach them".

title: OPINION: Higher education has many important stories to tell. So, let’s hear them
summary:
Higher education is at least partly responsible for its slide in public trust and perceived value to society. It needs to act now to restore confidence in its usefulness. The loss of trust is real and across the board. The proportion of Americans who say a college education is “very important” has dropped to an […]

The post OPINION: Higher education has many important stories to tell. So, let’s hear them appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
Higher education is at least partly responsible for its slide in public trust and perceived value to society. It needs to act now to restore confidence in its usefulness.

The loss of trust is real and across the board. The proportion of Americans who say a college education is “very important” has dropped to an all-time low of 31 percent, according to a 2026 Gallup poll. This was a four-percentage-point drop since 2025 and the lowest share since Gallup first asked the question in 1978. As recently as 2013, 70 percent of Americans in a Gallup survey said college was “very important.”

However, every semester, in a course I teach on reputation management, when I have my students do a SWOT (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats) analysis on themselves and ask about their most important strength, they invariably answer something along the lines of, “being at a university, learning how to learn and preparing myself for an uncertain future.”

Related: Interested in innovations in higher education? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter.

Americans in general, like my students, still value higher education’s ability to deliver certain outcomes: A Lumina-Gallup survey in 2025 found that a solid majority of Americans believed that higher education drives innovation, helps create businesses and leads to better jobs.

The research shows that two things can be true at the same time: “I have less trust in your value than I did; you’re still important to me.”

Many institutions implicitly assumed that their value was obvious. They believed that if they kept doing what they’d been doing, all would be fine. To maintain those beliefs, they had to ignore early warning signs, visible before Donald Trump’s second presidency, that foretold a full-scale assault on higher education’s value.

President Trump, from his bully pulpit, has regularly made deeply incomplete or blatantly false claims about higher education that have proved highly damaging. Higher ed leaders have yet to offer an effective response or strategy.

Other American institutions have also recently suffered a loss of public trust, but this should be of little consolation and is no excuse for inaction.

Asked recently at a public forum whether he’d seen any effort by his peers to organize for collective action on unified messaging about, for example, higher ed’s return on investment, the president of a liberal arts college said that he had seen none.

This is despite the fact that higher ed has great stories to tell about itself. Major urban campuses, for example, have worked closely with industries to teach students new manufacturing and management techniques; land-grant colleges helped farmers improve their crops and then evolved into public universities that send hundreds of thousands of graduates into the workforce each year.

Institutions can also point to their role in helping students become better human beings and citizens through the liberal arts. Thomas Jefferson and other Founders saw the purpose of higher education as sustaining democracy by creating better citizens. The stories higher ed tells, like ancient myths, can capture and convey important societal values.

Related: Experts say higher education is an industry in turmoil. The collateral damage is widespread

Here’s what we in higher ed can do to restore confidence and prevent additional erosion. First is to acknowledge that there is a problem and that many citizens don’t know about the contributions higher education makes to their community, state, country and world.

Second is to find the right messages, hopefully ones that are simple and reflect the core of the benefits produced. Doing so requires that higher ed leaders resist the tendency to say, “We’re already doing that!” — because the reality is, we’re not doing enough, and we’re not doing it often enough.

One message among others that could resonate is to highlight the many ways that higher education makes the lives of Americans better — by earning new patents in science and technology, conducting basic research, engineering innovations, fostering student internships, improving public policy and much more. We do these things every day. Faculty do them. Students do them. Graduates really do them.

An affordable approach is to inject those how-we-make-life-better messages into existing communication vehicles and channels. A clever example is a Facebook video series from American University in which its president makes FaceTime calls to undergraduates. In a recent one, he called a student whose university-funded internship in Los Angeles had him helping a city department design a new system for tracking citizen requests.

The video checks a number of boxes: It shows a student involved in real-world problem-solving while boosting his future job prospects, and it showcases the importance of paid internships. It also reveals a social benefit for city residents and highlights a college president who knows and cares about the impact academic programs can have.

There is an endless list of possible positive stories to tell. We could talk about colleges’ community engagement work and partnerships with groups and businesses, new majors, members of the military returning to school, first-generation students and recent legal immigrants attending college.

So let’s do a better job of communicating the important public good we do every day and tell our own stories of how we’ve faced obstacles, transformed ourselves, dealt with conflict, helped society, supported democracy and ultimately triumphed in the best tradition of the mythic hero’s journey.

Doug Barry is a board member of AltLiberalArts, a nonprofit that supports the teaching of the liberal arts. He also teaches reputation management at George Washington University.

Contact the opinion editor at opinion@hechingerreport.org.

title: New Zealand’s Opportunity party takes aim at populist politics as it prepares to enter parliament
summary:
Minor party leader Qiulae Wong says ‘populism doesn’t deliver results’ and that her vision for a low emissions future will drive its talks with major parties

A history-making centrist party that could influence New Zealand’s political direction has taken aim at populism as lawmakers arrived at parliament on Monday.

A nail-biting election failed to hand either the incumbent rightwing coalition or opposition left bloc a strong winning hand on Saturday. New Zealanders will now need to wait until 27 November for the final result, which includes the addition of about 400,000 “special votes” – those cast overseas or outside the voter’s electorate.

full_text:
A history-making centrist party that could influence New Zealand’s political direction has taken aim at populism as lawmakers arrived at parliament on Monday.

A nail-biting election failed to hand either the incumbent rightwing coalition or opposition left bloc a strong winning hand on Saturday. New Zealanders will now need to wait until 27 November for the final result, which includes the addition of about 400,000 “special votes” – those cast overseas or outside the voter’s electorate.

The Opportunity party, led by businesswoman Qiulae Wong, secured 5.9% of the party votes, clearing the hurdle to enter parliament, and becoming the first new party not born of an existing MP, or party, to enter parliament since the formation of New Zealand’s mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system in 1996.

Wong, who is of Chinese and European descent, also becomes the first leader of a party who has Asian ethnicity.

With the left and right blocs separated by just a few seats, after the official results are released, Opportunity could be in a position to decide who governs.

On Monday, newly elected lawmakers descended on Wellington for their induction into parliament, including Opportunity’s seven MPs. From parliament’s steps, Wong said it was “a huge day” for the party, whose nearly 150,000 supporters wanted a more pragmatic approach to politics.

“We’ve seen that populism doesn’t deliver results,” she said. “It is paper thin, it doesn’t have substance around taking countries forward. So it’s really encouraging to have had that support.”

Opportunity will negotiate first with the party that secures the highest number of seats, but its vision for a low-emissions future, and an inclusive New Zealand, will drive its final decision. Its five bottom-line issues include action on New Zealand’s supermarket duopoly, capping political donations, a 10-year cross-party plan for health, ending bottom trawling in the fishing industry and strengthening New Zealand’s climate commitments.

“Ultimately, we need to align on that future vision for New Zealand,” Wong said.

Leader of the centre-right National party, Christopher Luxon, had previously ruled out working with Opportunity but he extended an olive branch on Monday. Speaking to RNZ, Luxon said he would call Wong “shortly” and discuss the need for cross-party collaboration.

“I intend to build a relationship with her and try and find common ground with her, too,” Luxon said.

National, and Labour – the centre-left mainstream party – experienced a near photo-finish on Saturday, with neither party clearing 30% of the vote. The two parties recorded their worst combined vote in MMP history.

In contrast, minor parties hoovered up support, amid public frustration with persistently high living costs and incrementalist policymaking. The Greens and Act both claimed their highest ever results, while New Zealand First jumped nearly 4% from its 2023 result. Te Pāti Māori also managed to retain five electorate seats, despite major challenges and in-fighting over the past year.

But while the minor parties celebrate their successes, New Zealand is reckoning with the aftermath of the messy election result, which is not only on track to deliver the second lowest voter turnout ever, but has triggered questions about the future of New Zealand’s voting system.

In New Zealand, voters cast two votes: one for an electorate MP and one for a party. The system is meant to produce a parliament that reflects each party’s share of the nationwide vote. However, if New Zealanders vote for more electorate MPs from a particular party than their party vote would entitle them to, they get to keep the extra MPs in what is called an overhang.

As it stands, New Zealand’s parliament could have an additional eleven overhang seats, because National and Te Pāti Māori gained more electorates than their share of the popular vote.

Political scientists say the complexities around overhang seats raise serious questions about MMP.

“It kind of starts to defeat the purpose of MMP,” says Dr Lara Greaves, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington, who edited a textbook on MMP.

Te Pāti Māori had campaigned for people to only give them their electorate vote, to engineer an overhang in the seven Māori electorates. So far, they’re on track for five seats.

Meanwhile, various right wing groups, including one backed by wealthy businessman Harry Mowbray, had asked supporters to party vote for the Act of NZ First parties, while backing National electorate MPs to engineer overhangs on the right. So far, National could have six overhang seats.

Greaves said such campaigns undermined the spirit of MMP, which New Zealanders voted for in the 1990s after a string of skewed results under the first past the post system.

“I am concerned these sorts of issues could create further polarisation,” Greaves said.

“The possibility is some people will be quite unsettled by this result … there might be questions as to the legitimacy of this whole parliament and this government.”

title: ‘A global political awakening’: how gen Z protests are sweeping the world
summary:
From Serbia to Bangladesh and India to France, young people are pushing back against authoritarianism and reshaping political landscapes

In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard.

Both movements burst into international public view last month as they became central during election campaigns to the pushback against authoritarianism. What they also offered, however, was a window into a wider phenomenon playing out across the globe, as youth-led movements reshape political landscapes.

full_text:
In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard.

Both movements burst into international public view last month as they became central during election campaigns to the pushback against authoritarianism. What they also offered, however, was a window into a wider phenomenon playing out across the globe, as youth-led movements reshape political landscapes.

“Gen Z is rising,” said Erica Chenoweth, a political scientist at Harvard Kennedy School. “It is abundantly clear that a significant proportion of gen Z is tired of sitting on the sidelines while their political systems fail them.”

Researchers have documented at least 25 protests around the world in which this age group – roughly those between the ages of 14 and 29 – has played a role.

From Bangladesh to Belgium and Italy to India, it seems gen Z, who account for about a third of the world’s population, have found their voice. “Gen Z may be experiencing a global political awakening,” Chenoweth wrote in a recent essay.

Their reasons for taking to the streets have varied widely, from protesting against corruption and an unequal playing field to calling for more investment in education, affordable housing and action on the climate crisis.

Many of the first protests to make waves were in Asia and Africa. In 2024, students in Dhaka, Bangladesh, made global headlines after they pulled off what was described as the world’s first successful gen Z-led revolution.

The protests began over a quota law but swiftly snowballed into a wider show of discontent against the increasingly autocratic rule of the prime minister, Sheikh Hasina. Two months later, Hasina resigned and fled the country by helicopter after being, as the Associated Press reported, “chased out by young protesters”.

Two years later and 4,000 miles away, students were at the helm of another revolution in Serbia, pushing back against a government that had steadily tightened its grip on the media and stuffed institutions with party loyalists.

Late last month, Serbia’s students’ movement was catapulted from the streets to the halls of power as they ousted Aleksandar Vučić in elections, bringing an end to his party’s 14 years in power.

Students and young people have long been at the forefront of the push for change, the analysts Cait Dallaire and Sebastian Dittgen wrote recently, citing the US civil rights movement and the 2011 Arab spring.

“What is unique about the current movement is the infrastructure of mobilisation: TikTok and X amplify and accelerate grievances; Discord servers and group chats enable decentralised planning; virtual private networks and mirrored content help organisers circumvent internet shutdowns,” they said.

It was this potent combination – young people in the streets and social media – that helped drive Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s comeback to win Brazil’s presidential election last month. After a bruising loss in the first round to the rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, there was dismay in the country’s political left.

That was until students from the Fluminense Federal University mobilised in a pro-Lula march, setting off a wave of similar actions across the country. Soon after, the congressman and Lula ally André Janones, 42, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” that attracted millions of people looking to help boost pro-Lula content on social media.

On the night of his victory, Lula recognised their power. “I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” he said.

Some politicians have sought to engage gen Z from the start. In the US, Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for New York mayor combined a canny use of social media with a legion of about 50,000 volunteers that had young people at its heart. The New York Times wrote that “volunteering for Mr Mamdani’s campaign became a salve” for young New Yorkers as the campaign became not just about “mobilising, but socialising”.

It was a nod to the global context in which many gen Zers have come of age; one riven by conflicts such as the Israel-Gaza war, the escalating climate crisis and the rise of nationalism, while the rules that have shaped the international order since the second world war are fraying.

In recent weeks, youth-led protests have begun to sweep Europe, from school students in France demanding better conditions in which to work to those in Spain who pitched tents to rally for affordable housing. In Germany, thousands of people took to the streets to protest against the cost of living and call for more investment in education, health and climate action in a movement organised by a group calling itself Gen Z regelt!, or Gen Z will sort this.

Analysts have been swift to point to the link between the protests. “The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs, told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “In Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”

A similar note of disillusionment threads through India’s Cockroach movement, which began as an online satire and has since swelled into a show of force against the strongman government of Narendra Modi. Fuelled by social media and rooted in democratic ideals, the power of the movement was laid bare this summer after Cockroach-led protests forced the resignation of the country’s education minister.

Equally visible is the pushback by India’s security forces against the movement, detaining thousands, unleashing teargas and beating people with lathis, or wooden clubs. Authorities went to extreme lengths in October to keep them from gathering in central Delhi, barricading roads and shutting down the internet and public transport.

It was a window into another facet that has defined youth-led protests, as research suggests they tend to be met with higher levels of repression, despite the fact that they are no more likely to use violence than others.

In France, lawyers and rights groups say several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons. After the 2024 protests in Bangladesh, UN human rights experts said as many as 1,400 people had been killed, mostly by security forces, while thousands more suffered severe, often life-altering injuries.

In a recent analysis, Civicus, a non-profit that monitors global civic freedoms, said: “Because they question the distribution of economic and political power, gen Z-led protests have invariably been met with state violence,” linking the violence meted out to young protesters with their focus on systems and institutions that have long been generally accepted.

In Morocco, more than 2,000 people were charged and many received harsh prison sentences after a 2025 movement known as Gen Z 212 targeted officials over corruption, neglected public services and the lack of opportunities. Weeks later, in Mexico, youth-led protests over corruption and crime led to clashes with police in which dozens of people were arrested.

The outcomes of both of these movements show the varying success of gen Z protests. But at times, the foundations laid in one protest have given rise to others. In the US, much of today’s youth organising was shaped by the pro-Palestine student movement, in which there were thousands of arrests, expulsions and suspensions. Many schools instated anti-protest policies amid a broader rollback of educational freedom on campus.

Students, however, have continued to push for change. Last month hundreds in North Carolina marched in the heat to the polls after their historically Black university was denied a polling site, while thousands across the country have responded to the Cornell 7 case by skipping class, protesting and launching occupations.

As Chenoweth of the Harvard Kennedy School noted, the wave of recent youth-led protests may mark the beginning of a “profound generational transformation in world affairs” – one that could be capable of countering the global trend of democratic backsliding.

Ultimately, however, as Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris recently told the Associated Press, the explosion of youth movements across Europe hints at a wider truth that has long been overlooked across the globe.

“We all agree on one point,” he said. “That young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”

title: University libraries are being swarmed by AI bots, putting public access at risk
summary: Academic libraries are fighting off swarms of data-scraping bots — that are slowing or crashing sites meant for students, researchers and the public — as AI companies continue hunting for content to feed their large language models.
full_text:
Academic libraries are fighting off swarms of data-scraping bots — that are slowing or crashing sites meant for students, researchers and the public — as AI companies continue hunting for content to feed their large language models.

University libraries say entire collections are being knocked offline by persistent streams of unruly bots trying to access their archives, which include academic, historical and government documents.

"They're just out there on the internet, just bombarding us with trying to grab up as much material as possible," Jill Strykowski, cataloguing and government documents lead at San Jose State University, told CBC News.

The bots are used by both AI and third-party companies to scour websites and retrieve data, often to feed LLMs like Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT.

Libraries, museums and other cultural heritage institutions are prime targets because they have quality, vetted information that is generally not hidden behind paywalls or logins.

The bots are "causing an incredible amount of work and headache for every institution that does digitization work and every institution that is trying to make information openly available," Strykowski says.

Researchers found such reports started appearing in late 2024 across North America, Europe and Oceania and experts tell CBC News the problem continues to get worse.

And new challenges keep arising, says Dean Seeman, director of collections and digital infrastructure at University of Victoria Libraries.

"Sometimes the bot traffic gets so bad that it causes the sites to go down completely for a little while," he said.

Seeman says this creates a "real problem" for public access.

Regular people using library websites are now, effectively, in competition with infinite traffic from bot farms, says Peter Lewis, Canada Research Chair in Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence at Ontario Tech University.

"This is another instance of large, private companies making use of common-good public interest institutions in a way that's very extractive and just assumes that that stuff is available and is free — and then using it to be able to produce highly commercial models that then they can go and sell back to people," he said.

Good bots and bad bots

Eric Hellman, executive director of Project Gutenberg — a U.S.-based volunteer organization that digitizes and archives cultural works and distributes eBooks — wrote in a blog last year that these bots, which he characterizes as poorly programmed "monstrosities," are "destroying open access" on the internet.

He tells CBC News that "everything's gotten worse" since he wrote that.

Hellman says the problem comes down to good bots and bad bots.

He explains that search engines like Google, and archiving sites like Internet Archive, use bots that follow robots.txt — voluntary sets of instructions on websites that tell them what they can and can't do, so they don't disrupt the site's functioning while gathering information.

AI scraping bots, on the other hand, sometimes ignore these rules and overwhelm websites — in some cases requesting thousands of documents a second and downloading them in every available format.

As an example, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill reported last year that it received more than 11,000 searches for Finnish music from thousands of different internet addresses on the same day. The university said its library catalogue was periodically shutting out students, faculty and staff due to bot traffic.

And because one company or bot farm can work from thousands of IP addresses, Hellman says the old fix of blocking problematic IPs is no longer useful.

He says Project Gutenberg is happy for its materials to be used as AI training data and even offers a one-click download of its entire library of books, "but the bots are too stupid to use it."

"Our material is almost all public domain material. It's exactly the sort of material that they should be training on," he said. "We just wish they would do it in a respectful way that doesn't take down websites."

Open access a 'huge benefit'

Some libraries have set up CAPTCHA challenges or other verification systems to weed out bots.

The problem is, those measures can also weed out the good bots, says Michael Weinberg, co-director of GLAM-E, a collaborative academic initiative at NYU Law School and the University of Warwick focused on open-access policies for cultural institutions.

Some libraries have also begun to require login credentials, a controversial move that those who spoke to CBC News say they want to avoid because it puts barriers on human access to things they believe should be easily accessible.

And as the scraping bots get more advanced, experts say they could also learn to work around these strategies.

Major AI firms have argued that scraping publicly available data to train their models is permissible under fair use and in the public's best interest.

But faced with widespread criticism and copyright lawsuits, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Microsoft expressed support last week for honouring a single, standardized opt-out signal in a website's robots.txt file that could block their web crawlers from harvesting data.

Compliance would be voluntary, however, and the agreement leaves out problematic bots from third-party companies and smaller AI startups.

Weinberg says the digitization of valuable information has been a "fantastic" development for humanity — giving researchers, teachers and curious citizens easy access to resources that, 20 years ago, "would have required driving or flying or a special permission to get access."

Organizations like GLAM-E are trying to figure out long-term solutions to preserve that access for humans and helpful bots alike.

Right now, the bots create "a disincentive for libraries and other institutions to make parts of their collection available online," Weinberg said. "I think it's been a huge benefit to society that libraries and museums and other cultural institutions have put a huge amount of work into making their collections available."

full_text:
We are at a pivotal moment in education. The rise of generative AI has forced a widespread re-evaluation of how we assess student learning. For decades, the take-home essay, the research paper, and the report have been mainstays of assessment—primarily “product-based” assignments where the final artifact is the main object of evaluation.

AI directly challenges this model by making the production of polished text, code, or images trivial. The question facing college and university faculty is not whether to address this reality, but how to respond with intention. The AI-Resistant Pedagogy Studio is my attempt to provide a practical, structured answer—one grounded in a framework that centers the uniquely human journey of learning.

The honest origin of this resource is simpler than any theoretical framework. Faculty kept coming to me with the same question: “How do I get my students to stop using AI?” I understood the frustration behind it. But I also knew that policing students into compliance was not a pedagogy—it was a surveillance strategy. And contestability—the exhausting back-and-forth of trying to prove whether a student used AI—was consuming faculty energy that belonged in the classroom. So instead of asking how we stop students from using AI, I started asking a different question: what would we have to design so that the learning itself could not be outsourced? That reframe became the Studio. I built it as a free, openly licensed OER resource because I did not want cost or access to be the barrier between a faculty member and a better approach. Every instructor deserves a practical starting point, not just a policy to enforce.

What the Studio Is

The AI-Resistant Pedagogy Studio: An Interactive Toolkit for Assignment Redesign is a living document—hosted at https://ynaqbxzy.manus.space/ and regularly updated with current research and vetted best practices—that I developed and published in 2025 (Evans, 2026). It is organized into eight sections: Overview, In the News, Tool Landscape, Framework, Strategies, Best Practices, Case Studies, and a hands-on interactive Toolkit.

Its core premise: as AI tools become more prevalent, our role as educators shifts. We are not just imparting knowledge—we are fostering human capacities that resist automation. The strength of our communities—our classrooms, our departments, our institutions—is our greatest asset in this work.

Since its release, the Studio has been adopted as a faculty development resource at institutions across the country. These include Clemson University, South Dakota University, Washington University, Hood College, the University of Houston-Downtown, Loyola-Notre Dame, and Roman University—each using the Studio to train faculty on redesigning assignments that are resilient to generative AI, shifting their professional development programs away from detection and toward intentional pedagogical design. The Studio has also reached beyond traditional higher education: it was featured on page 7 of the American Art Therapy Association (AATA) Undergraduate Art Therapy Educators Newsletter, where practitioners highlighted its value for deepening the human connections and critical thinking central to their field (AATA Newsletter, 2026). That the Studio has found traction in art therapy education, research universities, liberal arts colleges, and Hispanic-Serving Institutions alike speaks to something universal in the problem it addresses: faculty everywhere are asking the same question, and they need more than a policy in response.

From Product to Process: The Central Shift

The Studio is built around a necessary and accelerated shift toward process-based assessment. This approach emphasizes the uniquely human journey of learning: the research process, the collaborative dialogue, the critical self-reflection, and the iterative development of an idea. The focus moves from “what did you produce?” to “how did you learn, and what can you do with that knowledge?” (Evans, 2026).

When AI can produce a satisfactory first draft in seconds, the skills that become more valuable are those AI struggles with: critical evaluation of AI-generated content, creative synthesis of multiple sources, ethical reasoning, and personal reflection. Practically, process-based assessment means building systems that value:

Multi-stage assignments—proposals, annotated bibliographies, drafts, and final versions—that make the research process visible and gradable

Oral defenses or brief one-on-one conferences that verify individual understanding and ensure knowledge resides with the student, not the tool

AI critique tasks: having students analyze AI-generated output for flaws, biases, and weaknesses (Cornell University, n.d.)

Community-based and experiential projects grounded in local, real-world contexts where AI cannot physically participate

Three Core Strategies for AI-Resistant Design

The Studio organizes its assignment redesign framework around three strategies, each targeting something AI genuinely cannot replicate.

1. Collaborative Inquiry

Assignments requiring genuine, interdependent collaboration—where the process of interaction and shared knowledge construction is as important as the product. AI struggles with the nuanced, dynamic, and often messy process of real human interaction, negotiation, and shared ownership. Practical examples include jigsaw presentations, team-based learning structures, and structured peer review of drafts (Evans, 2026).

2. Authentic Engagment

Assignments that connect learning to real-world contexts, lived experiences, and tangible community needs. AI lacks lived experience, embodied knowledge, sensory perception, and the ability to navigate the unpredictable complexities of the real world. Oral history interviews, community-partner projects, and primary source fieldwork all require students to gather information no AI model can access (Evans, 2026).

3. Metacognitive Reflection

Assignments that require students to reflect on their own learning process, document their thinking, and critically evaluate their methods and tools. AI cannot engage in genuine self-reflection or authentic introspection about its own learning journey. Learning portfolios with reflection essays, process documentation projects, and AI usage and ethics reflections all center this uniquely human capacity (Evans, 2026).

The Equity Dimension

No discussion of AI-resistant pedagogy is complete without addressing equity. A reliance on technology can exacerbate the digital divide, disadvantaging students without reliable access to high-speed internet or modern devices. Furthermore, since many AI models are trained on biased data, their outputs can reinforce harmful stereotypes (Frontiers in Education, 2024; Shelton & Lanier, 2024).

The Studio addresses this directly: an equitable approach requires designing assessments that do not depend on premium AI tools and explicitly teaching students to identify and critique algorithmic bias. This means designing for the baseline—if a tool is not institutionally provided, it should not be required for the grade. It also means advocating for campus-wide licenses and providing dedicated in-class lab time so access does not determine academic success (Evans, 2026).

In my own work leading the Center for Teaching Excellence at Our Lady of the Lake University, an HSI institution, this equity lens is not optional—it is foundational. The Studio’s framework was built with under-resourced students and under-supported faculty explicitly in mind.

Redefining Academic Integrity

The focus of academic integrity is moving beyond a narrow definition of plagiarism toward a broader concept of ethical and transparent use of tools. Rather than simply banning AI, institutions are developing policies that require students to acknowledge and document their use of AI—shifting the conversation from “did you cheat?” to “how did you use this tool responsibly?” This requires a culture of honesty built on proactive pedagogy rather than reactive detection (Packback, 2025; Sabourin Laflamme & Bruneault, 2025).

Practically, this means building in AI disclosure statements, requiring prompt histories alongside final submissions, and explaining the pedagogical rationale behind assignments so students understand what skills they are developing—and why those skills matter in a world with AI.

Faculty Development as the Engine of Change

Educators cannot be expected to navigate this new landscape alone. There is an urgent need for intentional, institutionally supported faculty development—training that goes beyond demonstrating how to use a new tool and focuses instead on pedagogical redesign and fair assessment strategy (Kolomitro & Schultz, 2024; Educause, 2024).

This is the work I do. Through conference presentations at venues including the NISOD Virtual Conference, the Northeast OER Summit, the Rutgers Online Learning Conference, the Innovative Teaching & Learning Conference, and the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board’s Digital Learning Summit, I have brought the Studio’s framework to faculty across disciplines and institution types. Additional engagements have included Educause, the University of Rhode Island, and the University of Tennessee.

When I present the Studio, I organize sessions around a single provocation: your current assignments may be measuring AI fluency, not student learning. From there, participants audit their existing assignments, anchor each to its underlying human-centric learning objective, and use the Studio’s interactive toolkit to rebuild around process, context, and verification.

What Faculty Can Do Now

The Studio is designed for incremental implementation. Three starting points any instructor can act on immediately:

Add one process checkpoint to an existing assignment. Ask students to submit a prompt history or a brief reflection log alongside their final draft. This alone shifts the locus of accountability.

Introduce one locally-grounded or experiential activity per unit. Field observations, community interviews, and maker projects are inherently AI-resistant because they require physical presence and specific context.

Replace a detection-focused policy with a disclosure-focused one. Shift from “prove you didn’t use AI” to “show me how you used AI and what you did with its output.”

Reclaiming the Classroom as a Human Space

The goal of AI-resistant pedagogy is not to win an arms race with technology. It is to reclaim the classroom as a space where the process of learning is just as valuable as the final product. By focusing on intentional design, critical empathy, and equitable access, we can build courses where AI becomes a legitimate collaborator in learning—not a shortcut around it.

The full Studio, including its interactive assignment redesign toolkit, case studies, and downloadable resources, is freely available at https://ynaqbxzy.manus.space/. It is a practitioner-first resource built to reduce manual instructional labor while strengthening the human core of every course.

Stacy Ybarra Evans, EdD, is a San Antonio-based educator and instructional strategist specializing in the integration of emerging technologies and AI-resistant pedagogy within higher education. She currently serves on the SXSW EDU 2026 Advisory Board and the Macmillan Accessibility Advisory Board, where she helps shape the future of educational content and inclusivity. Her approach focuses on bridging the gap between rapidly evolving generative AI tools and traditional learning objectives to ensure authentic student engagement. Her expertise is further grounded in her role as a Quality Matters Master Reviewer, ensuring that innovative course design meets the highest national standards for digital learning and academic integrity.

title: Professional Ecosystems: Harmonious Alignment for Faculty Service

full_text:
As faculty members, we often discuss the pressures of the classroom and research; yet, the demands of service remain largely overlooked. Junior faculty, in particular, can feel compelled to join committees, spearhead university initiatives, lead student organizations, and foster community partnerships. This burden is even heavier for those from marginalized or underrepresented backgrounds, who often find themselves conforming to molds not built for them. Whether joining prestigious but unfulfilling committees or executing a senior faculty’s community project, these performative tasks often lead to burnout and isolation. Ultimately, these systemic pressures drive talented faculty to leave their universities-or higher education all together.

Cultivating Professional Ecosystems

In their book, Good Work: When Excellence and Ethics Meet, Howard Gardner, Mihaly Csikszentmhalyi, and William Damon pose a question that sparked a transformative journey for me: What can people do when conditions threaten a harmonious alignment? Reflecting on this prompted me to interrogate my own burnout and reimagine how to nurture my love for the academic community around me. From this experience, I developed the Professional Ecosystem Framework. This framework is designed to guide faculty in cultivating their own service focus by emphasizing belonging, reclaiming, and healing. It consists of three strata – a term chosen over “components” or “elements” to evoke the geological and ecological layers that inherently support one another. The three strata that intertwine to create the Professional Ecosystem Framework are:

Living Arbors: Unearthing Radical Belonging with Ancestral Roots – This stratum of the framework moves beyond the idea of a network and encourages faculty to see themselves as a canopy. Within this stratum, we create shade for others while ensuring their own roots have the space to drink.

Un-Grafted Seeds: Nurturing Self in Sovereign Soil – In horticulture, grafting forces a vine onto foreign roots. However, this stratum of the framework is about embracing your ancestral soil, nurturing your lived experiences, and showcasing your unique strengths.

Reciprocal Harvests: Envisioning Praxis as Medicine – Work that feeds the community must also feed the worker. This stratum redefines productivity as a cycle of communal empowerment and personal healing.

Theoretical Foundations

The roots of the Professional Ecosystem Framework are planted within two theoretical perspectives. The first theoretical perspective shaping the framework is Chicana feminism. This theoretical perspective guides the framework’s emphasis on the collective, spiritual, and familial aspects of service (Anzaldúa, 1987; Garcia, 2014). Within this also exists a heightened awareness that our experiences are often rooted in resistance that is gendered, racial, and class-based (Bernal, 1998).

The second theoretical perspective nurturing the framework is the Relational Indigenous Leadership Philosophy (RILP) developed by Hardison-Stevens (2022). This philosophy has tribal ways of knowing affiliated with the Omushkeg Cree-Metis, Ojibway, Cowlitz, and Stilacoom peoples. The RILP first acknowledges that our sensory awareness guides us through spaces not created for us. Rather than focusing on authoritative hierarchies or Eurocentric views of knowledge, RILP emphasizes self-advocacy, community well-being, and stewardship.

Developing Your Own Professional Ecosystem

Stratum 1: Living Arbors

My grandmother once spoke to me of human towers or castells, which come from a Catalonian tradition where humans stand on the shoulders of others in order to create a tower that stands over a hundred feet tall. She reminded me that the most important part of the tower is not the victorious individual at the top; rather, it is the people who are at the bottom. Starting the journey to build my own ecosystem required a re-evaluation of my human tower. My colleagues often looked upward towards those at the top with institutional power, but I knew I had to return to my roots and pay attention to those at the foundation of my tower. I had shamefully neglected my relationships with aunties, cousins, or fiends who lacked formal university educations. In healing those connections, I discovered that their insights are as essential to my academic journey as any institutional guidance or alliances.

As you reflect on your human tower, consider reflecting on the following: Who is woven into your ecosystem and who has been overlooked? As a faculty member, you know that having a department chair or dean in your corner is powerful. However, when you tap into the ancestral roots of your background and invite individuals from your past into your current academic life, new growth begins. This new growth creates a canopy of protection not only for yourself but also for others who come from similar backgrounds.

Stratum 2: Un-Grafted Seeds

The next stratum of the framework was more challenging for me. I was caught up in the comparison game and compared my service and leadership to colleagues around me. I finally engaged in introspection and identified unique skills I bring to the table. For example, I had been a single mother, and I had lived on government assistance. These aspects of my life had cultivated unique skills many of my colleagues did not have.

As you reflect on your uniqueness, consider reflecting on the following: What lived experiences have cultivated strengths, and how might these strengths serve you in academia? If you are struggling to answer some of these questions, considering exploring the community cultural wealth model (Yosso & Burciaga, 2016). Her model considers different aspects of capital that are often overlooked in Eurocentric spaces. As you explore this second stratum of the framework, remind yourself that the goal is not to graft onto a foreign root but to allow your unique lived experiences nurture authentic strengths.

Stratum 3: Reciprocal Harvests

Reflecting on the first two strata solidified my decision to change my service focus. I began to envision my own praxis as medicine for myself and others. While the other service areas at my university were worthwhile, they did not resonate with me. I sought out initiatives that promoted healing myself and others, leading me to establishing a campus clothing closet for students, assisting parenting students, and developing a mentorship program for Latinas.

As you cultivate this stratum of the framework, consider asking yourself- How can I advocate for students in ways I wish someone had advocated for me, and how can I turn that into initiatives that nurture my academic community? As mentioned earlier, work that feeds the community must also feed the worker. This last stratum of the framework allows you to still be productive but within communal spaces of care.

Conclusion

We must move from a culture that consumes its members to one that cultivates them. Like the strata of the forest or the earth on which we stand, having a professional ecosystem creates an intertwining layer of support. Rather than engaging in the competitive nature of higher education, which can often make you feel like you are being eaten alive, we can shift the culture to one of curious cultivation. By modeling our own professional ecosystem, we do more than just survive the pressures of higher education, we become a part of the transformation for others.

Aimée Myers, PhD, is an Associate Professor of Literacy and Language at Texas Woman’s University. She also serves as the Associate Dean of Academic Affairs in the College of Professional Education. Her teaching specialization focuses on culturally responsive-sustaining practices. In her research, she works to utilize social constructivist, decolonized approaches with underserved populations. Her current studies include visual testimonios with immigrant and refugee students and community cultural wealth with graduate students from underrepresented backgrounds. She is the coordinator of the COPE Clothing Closet, the founder of the Latinx Juntos Mentorship program, and the facilitator for the Urban Education Microcredential.

title: Digitale Bildungsangebote zu DDR, Mauerbau und Mauerfall
summary: Zeitzeugenberichte, Videos, Graphic Novel, 360-Grad-Rundgänge, AR-Apps & Co.: ein Überblick über digitale Angebote, die die deutsche Teilung thematisieren.
full_text:
Inhaltsverzeichnis

close notice

This article is also available in English. It was translated with technical assistance and editorially reviewed before publication.

.

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Am 13. August 2026 jährte sich der Mauerbau bereits zum 65. Mal, am diesjährigen 9. November wird der Fall der Berliner Mauer zum 37. Mal gefeiert. Wer sich für die deutsch-deutsche Geschichte interessiert, findet mittlerweile zahlreiche kostenlose Onlineangebote. Sowohl Gedenkstätten, Museen, Stiftungen und Vereine als auch öffentlich-rechtliche Sender haben eine Vielzahl von Formaten entwickelt, die sich für verschiedene Altersklassen und Einsatzzwecke eignen, wie etwa den Schulunterricht. Dazu zählen frei zugängliche Onlinearchive mit Erklärvideos und -audios, interaktive Graphic Novels, immersive Lern- und Informations-Apps, 360-Grad-Lernräume oder auch Podcasts. Die im August erschienene AR-App zum Mauerbau von WDR und MDR ist eines der jüngsten Angebote dieser Art. Manche Angebote konzentrieren sich auf Mauer und Grenze, andere auch auf den DDR-Alltag unter der SED-Diktatur.

Fokus auf Mauergeschichten

Den stärksten Fokus auf die Mauergeschichte hat die Stiftung Berliner Mauer. Sie bündelt Onlineausstellungen etwa zur Fluchthilfe zwischen 1961 und 1989, einen Audio-Walk zum Checkpoint Charlie, Onlinetouren zur East Side Gallery, einen digitalen Tourguide mit vier Touren und mehr als 140 Ereignismarken sowie den Podcast „Grenzerfahrung“ von 2021.

Mit der umfangreichen Onlinesammlung, dem Fotoportal mauer-fotos.de und dem Portal Mauerspuren, über das Nutzer noch erhaltene Mauerreste melden können, lässt sich mit digitalisierten Quellen auch selbst recherchieren.

Verlinkt ist außerdem die unter anderem von der Bundeszentrale für politische Bildung (bpb) betriebene, barrierefreie Chronik der Mauer mit Dokumenten, Videos, Filmen und Zeitzeugeninterviews. Und auch 140 Mauertote haben dort jeweils einen eigenen Eintrag mit Porträts erhalten. Der unter „Chronik der Mauer“ zugängliche Lernbereich hält Arbeitsblätter für die Grundschule bis zur Sekundarstufe II bereit.

Die bpb bietet zudem mit der kostenlosen App „Die Berliner Mauer“ rund 250 Fotos, 25 Videos, 50 Tondokumente sowie geführte Touren zu mehr als 75 Orten an. Sie ist auch auf Englisch nutzbar, wie einige andere der hier vorgestellten Angebote.

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Möchten Lehrkräfte oder Erziehungsberechtigte Material und Dokumente je nach Klassenstufe oder auch Fachunterricht erhalten, bietet Planet Schule nach diesen Präferenzen zusammengestellte Sammlungen zum Themenschwerpunkt „Die DDR und der Mauerfall“ an. Außerdem steht dort das 2025 mit dem Grimme Online Award ausgezeichnete kostenfreie Story-Lernspiel „Herbst 89 – Auf den Straßen von Leipzig“ zur Verfügung, das vom Deutschen Historischen Museum und dem Spieleentwickler Playing History erstellt wurde.

Orte der Einheit und der Repression

Da sich Zeitgeschichte an vielen Orten noch vor Ort erkunden lässt, stellt die Stiftung Haus der Geschichte mit „Orte der Einheit“ 40 Orte der deutschen Geschichte nach 1989 in Berlin auf einer interaktiven Karte vor, mit Audiobeiträgen für zu Hause und unterwegs.

Und auch das inzwischen abgeschlossene Portal „Orte der Repression in SBZ und DDR“ der Stiftung Haus der Geschichte bündelt Gedenkstätten, Museen und historische Orte, die an Opfer politischer Verfolgung erinnern.

360-Grad-Grenzgeschichten und Grenzbegegnungen-Podcast

Das Grenzmuseum Schifflersgrund ergänzt seine Vor-Ort-Angebote um digitale Formate, die auch von zu Hause aus genutzt werden können. Das Grenzmuseum liegt an der thüringisch-hessischen Grenze und hat seine Lernangebote als 360-Grad-Umgebungen aufgebaut. „Grenzgeschichten“ umfasst zehn Lernräume aus hoch aufgelösten Panoramen, die sich am Tablet oder PC erkunden lassen. Darin stecken laut Museum mehr als 100 historische Quellen, etwa Zeitzeugeninterviews, Filme, Dokumente und Fotos, ergänzt um Quellenlisten und Experteninterviews. Inhaltlich geht es um Flucht, Zwangsaussiedlung, Grenztourismus und Jugend im Sperrgebiet. Das Projekt erhielt 2024 den DigAMus-Award.

Ein Modul führt Schülergruppen digital zur DDR-Staatssicherheit auf dem Lindenberg und bindet Videointerviews sowie pädagogische Aufgaben direkt ein.

- Die Brandenburger Aufarbeitungsbeauftragte stellt über das Zeitzeugenportal Brandenburg strukturierte Videointerviews mit Zeitzeuginnen und Zeitzeugen bereit. Schüler können Kurzbiografien, private Dokumente und Fotos analysieren.

- Die Stiftung Brandenburgische Gedenkstätten bietet Schulklassen ab Jahrgangsstufe 9 eine tabletbasierte Lern-App an, die in angemeldeten, pädagogisch begleiteten Workshops in den Gedenkstätten in Potsdam, Sachsenhausen oder Brandenburg (Havel) genutzt wird. Mittels der App können etwa Biografien im Zuchthaus Brandenburg-Görden, dem Untersuchungsgefängnis Potsdam (Leistikowstraße) und dem Speziallager Sachsenhausen digital erforscht werden.

- Die Gedenkstätte Berlin-Hohenschönhausen bietet Schulgruppen einen virtuellen 3D-Rundgang durch das ehemalige Stasi-Gefängnis, digitale Seminare und digitale Zeitzeugengespräche an. Details stehen auf der Website der Gedenkstätte.

- Mödlareuth ist ein Dorf mit rund 50 Einwohnern an der Grenze zwischen Bayern und Thüringen, das weltweite Bekanntheit als Symbol der deutschen Teilung erlangte – es wird deshalb auch „Little Berlin“ genannt. Auf der Website befinden sich einige historische Fotos der Teilung.
